text: Ethernet is the family of standards that defines how devices on a local network frame and transmit data at Layer 2 — the dominant wired LAN technology for decades, now running anywhere from 1 Gbps to 100 Gbps or more. Every network interface card has a MAC address burned into its hardware — a 48-bit identifier, written as six pairs of hex digits, where the first 24 bits identify the manufacturer and the last 24 make it unique.

A switch builds a MAC address table by learning: when a frame arrives on a port, the switch records which MAC address is reachable there. For a known destination, it forwards the frame out only that one port. For an unknown destination, it floods the frame out every other port — a one-time behavior, until it learns where that device actually lives.

That learn-then-forward behavior is why switches are dramatically more efficient and more secure than the hubs they replaced. A hub has no intelligence at all — it repeats every frame out every port, turning every device into something that can see all the traffic. A switch sends traffic only where it needs to go.

Hub, switch, and router aren't interchangeable terms. A hub operates at Layer 1 with no addressing intelligence. A switch operates at Layer 2, learning MAC addresses and forwarding selectively. A router operates at Layer 3, forwarding packets between different networks based on IP address — and routers are what actually separate one broadcast domain from another, since they don't forward broadcasts between networks.
